summary.summary: Bexley ended 2025/26 with £249.6m of debt (£224.6m long-dated PWLB at 3.34% plus £25m of short-term loans from other councils at an average 5.97%) against just £10.1m of investments, after cash balances more than halved in the year from £21.6m. The £25m of temporary borrowing was taken in February-March 2026 purely to keep the council liquid, at rates up to 7%, and all of it falls due in April 2026. The CFR outturn was £318.6m against £249.6m of borrowing, and the CIPFA liability benchmark shows existing loans are insufficient to meet the projected CFR, so more long-term borrowing is coming. All prudential limits were met and no limit was exceeded on any day.

news_drafts.headline: Bexley expects £22.456m government grant towards schools special needs deficit; council to fund £1.895m
news_drafts.lead:
Bexley Council's Cabinet was told on 21 October 2026 that the government's new High Needs Stability Grant is expected to cover £22.456m of the council's accumulated deficit on its dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools). The deficit sits in high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities. The grant is equivalent to 90% of the deficit as at 31 March 2026, after adjusting for £0.600m the council has already contributed.

The Department for Education expects the council ultimately to fund the remaining 10%, which is £1.895m, subject to further discussion. The grant is subject to approval of the SEND (special educational needs and disabilities) Reform Plan that the council has recently submitted, and would be received in 2026/27.

The grant replaces the Safety Valve agreement, a government arrangement that supported high needs spending and ended in March 2026. It brought £19.640m of additional government funding to Bexley from March 2023. The papers say the government has given no concrete indication of how deficits building up from April 2026 onwards will be addressed. The 2026/27 budget provides for a further in-year deficit of £22.473m on high needs.

news_drafts.headline: Bexley forecasts £479,000 overspend on special needs school transport, against £11.351m budget
news_drafts.lead:
Bexley Council expects to spend £11.830m this year on transport for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND), against a budget of £11.351m. That is an overspend of £0.479m, or 4.2%, according to the budget monitoring report (the in-year check of spending against budget) put to the Children's Services and Education Overview and Scrutiny Committee on 13 October 2026.

The report says the overspend reflects faster-than-projected growth in the number of children using travel assistance from September 2026. It links this to the council's SEND reform plan and to revised assumptions about personal transport budgets. The report's written commentary refers to a £0.387m variance for the service, forecast "to agree with the SEND reform plan growth and factoring in increase in demand from September 2026". The table in the same report shows £0.479m, the figure used here.

The council has agreed that SEN transport will be the subject of a "deep dive" analysis with its finance team to consider whether the budget should be adjusted. The papers do not say when that work will report back.

news_drafts.headline: Bexley eligible for grant covering 90% of its schools high needs deficit, subject to government approval of its SEND plan
news_drafts.lead:
Bexley would receive a grant covering 90% of its accumulated deficit on funding for children with special educational needs, if the government approves its reform plan. The borough's Schools Forum was told the council is eligible for a High Needs Stability Grant, payable in autumn 2026.

The deficit sits in the high needs part of the dedicated schools grant (DSG), the government grant that funds schools. High needs is the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities. The papers put the grant at 90% of the accumulated high needs deficit as at 31 March 2026. They do not give the deficit in pounds, and the grant is conditional: the council's paper says it is "subject to approval of the plan".

The plan is Bexley's Local SEND Reform Plan, which the council submitted to the Department for Education (DfE) on 19 June 2026. Decisions on plans were expected in September 2026. The paper presented to the forum describes the grant as resolving a material accumulated deficit in the high needs block.

The papers do not say whether the plan has yet been approved.

findings.headline: Capital programme forecast at £73.809m against £84.236m budget, £10.427m slippage (12.4%), with Highways delivering largest variance of £3.370m
findings.detail: The 2026/27 capital programme is forecast to underspend by £10.427m against the revised budget of £84.236m, with a forecast of £73.809m. Significant slippages include £3.370m for Highways and Street Scene (comprising £0.950m EV charging agreement delays, £0.751m road safety policy adoption delays, £0.700m bridge work access delays), £2.890m for BexleyCo (reprofiling and project delays), £1.280m for McKillops Way Travellers Site (slipped to 2027/28), and £1.551m for schools projects (SEN funding and capital maintenance).
findings.matters: Material capital slippage can indicate either planning/approvals delays (policy adoption, permitting) or execution challenges (contractor delays, cost inflation). The concentration in Highways and schools suggests either systemic delivery issues in those directorates or optimistic programming. A lender would want to understand whether this is one-off timing or a pattern that will recur in future years.
findings.figures: Forecast £73.809m vs budget £84.236m; £10.427m total slippage (12.4%); Highways/Street Scene £3.370m; BexleyCo £2.890m; McKillops Way £1.280m; schools projects £1.551m
findings.quote: £3.370m has slipped for Highways and Street Scene, the biggest variances being: £0.950m for Electric Vehicle charging due to delays in the agreement being signed, £0.751m on various schemes which need the Road Safety policy to be formally adopted first, and £0.700m for Bridge Joint Replacements due to on-street access delays.

findings.headline: High Needs Stability Grant to fund 90% of accumulated Dedicated Schools Grant deficit (£22.456m), with council to ultimately fund 10% (£1.895m), replacing ended Safety Valve agreement
findings.detail: The Safety Valve agreement that supported High Needs Block pressures ended in March 2026 after bringing £19.640m of additional government funding since March 2023. Government has now announced the High Needs Stability Grant, equivalent to 90% of the accumulated deficit as at 31 March 2026. For Bexley, this equates to £22.456m (after adjusting for £0.600m already contributed under Safety Valve). The 10% element that the DfE expects the council ultimately to fund is £1.895m. The government has given no concrete indication how deficits accumulating from April 2026 onwards will be addressed. The 2026/27 budget envisages a further in-year deficit of £22.473m.
findings.matters: This represents a structural shift from temporary Safety Valve funding toward quasi-permanent but contingent government funding, with a known future liability of £1.895m to be borne by the council. The ongoing in-year deficit of £22.473m suggests that High Needs pressures are not stabilizing. A lender would want to understand the council's plan for eventually meeting 100% of accumulated liabilities and trajectory of future in-year deficits.
findings.figures: High Needs Stability Grant: £22.456m (90% of deficit); council ultimate liability: £1.895m (10% of deficit); 2026/27 in-year deficit: £22.473m; Safety Valve funding 2023-2026: £19.640m total
findings.quote: The Government has announced the first phase of its new arrangements for supporting councils with High Needs deficits. Subject to approval of the recently submitted SEND Reform Plan, local authorities will be eligible to receive (in 2026/27) a new High Needs Stability Grant equivalent to 90% of their accumulated deficit as at 31 March 2026. After adjusting for the £0.600m of contributions that the council has already made to the deficit under Safety Valve, Bexley's expected High Needs Stability Grant allocation would be £22.456m. The 10% element of deficit which (subject to further discussion) the Department for Education expects the Council ultimately to fund would be £1.895m.

findings.headline: Bad debt provision forecast to increase by £5.778m (Collection Fund) and £0.117m net (General Fund), not yet reflected in current overspend forecast
findings.detail: Bad debt provision analysis shows material forecast increases not yet incorporated into the revenue forecast. Collection Fund bad debt (Council Tax and Business Rates, Bexley's share) is forecast to increase by £5.778m from £27.276m to £33.895m as at 31 March 2027. General Fund provision is forecast to increase by £0.117m net (or £0.848m gross before parking contributions). These are forecasts based on current debt levels and are explicitly stated as not included in the current forecast position.
findings.matters: Bad debt provisions are revenue expenditure that must be recognized in accounts. If these provisions materialize, they would convert the current £0.601m overspend into a material one of approximately £6m. A lender would want to understand why such a material provision increase is not yet reflected in the forecast and what is driving the debt accumulation.
findings.figures: Collection Fund provision increase forecast: £5.778m (from £27.276m to £33.895m); General Fund increase forecast: £0.117m net (from £12.376m to £12.661m); explicitly not included in current forecast
findings.quote: The table calculates that Bexley's share of the bad debt provision for the Collection Fund may need to increase by £5.778m as at 31 March 2027... The estimated movement is therefore not included in the current forecast.

findings.headline: Children's Services reporting two new high-cost LAC placements costing £1.130m for remainder of year, with placement contingency half-used
findings.detail: Children's Social Care is forecasting an overspend of £0.293m, an adverse movement of £0.376m since May. Two new high-cost looked-after children placements in recent weeks will cost £1.130m for the remainder of the financial year. The pressure is partially offset by an earlier-than-planned step-down of one child (£0.247m saving) and use of £0.600m of the contingency for new placements built into May. Remaining contingency for further new placements until March 2027 is now £0.600m, down from the original £1.200m.
findings.matters: High-cost LAC placement activity is volatile and hard-to-predict. The fact that half the annual contingency has been used in the first four months suggests remaining contingency may be insufficient, risking a further adverse movement in the second half of the year if additional high-cost placements are needed. A peer council would be interested in whether this reflects a systemic trend or isolated cases.
findings.figures: Two new placements: £1.130m for remainder of year; one step-down: £0.247m saving; contingency used: £0.600m of original £1.200m; remaining contingency: £0.600m
findings.quote: There have been two new high cost placements in recent weeks which together will cost £1.130m for the remainder of the financial year.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care client contributions review reveals trend of reduced income from service users, £0.377m adverse movement since May
findings.detail: Between May and July 2026, the council conducted a review of client contributions in Adult Social Care which revealed a trend of reduced income from service users. This £0.377m adverse movement is separate from, and in addition to, the £0.823m placement volume overspend. It points to either a demographic shift (more people unable to pay) or a change in assessment practices (fewer people deemed able to pay).
findings.matters: Client contributions offset the council's social care spending. A decline in contributions reduces the council's financial flexibility in its largest and most demographically pressured service area. A finance director or peer council would want to understand whether this is a temporary collection issue or a structural change in service user circumstances.
findings.figures: £0.377m adverse movement since May 2026/Period 2; trend of reduced income from service users
findings.quote: There has been a £0.377m adverse movement since May 2026/Period 2 because of a review of client contributions which is reflective of a trend of reduced income from service users.
